Michael Beer <Mi...@leila.ping.de> wrote:
> AFAIK, normal damage is dealt before aggro damage (thus maximizing the
> chance for a vamp to be burned) in the damage resolution phase.

It is all (typically) dealt simultaneously. But blood is burned to heal
the normal damage before any blood can be spent to prevent destruction
from the aggravated damage.

In short form: the normal damage is handled first.

The "applied simultaneously" part is important in allowing damage prevention
to be used against any of the damage - not just the normal part first.

The same.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at wrote:

> vte...@wizards.com (LSJ) wrote:
> > The ends-based explanation (by Gomi, I believe) is:
> >
> > A vampire with X blood who receives (and doesn't prevent) X+2 or more
> > damage, at least one point of which is aggravated, is burned.
> >
> > Restated:
> >
> > If a vampire takes X damage, at least 1 point of which is aggravated, then
> > he must burn X-1 blood or be burned.
>
> Can you please clarify: The first aggravated point doesn't burn any blood
> and sends the vamp to torpor. Right?

Doing things in terms of the "first" point is overly complicated, but since
you insist:

The first point of aggravated damage done to a vampire who is not
wounded (has healed all his damage so far) simply wounds the vampire
(since he cannot heal it). Since he cannot heal it, no blood is spent
to heal it. Since it will not destroy him, no blood is spent to prevent
destruction.

The first point of aggaravted damage done to a wounded vampire (one who
has not healed all of his damage so far - whether normal damage in
excess of blood or aggravated damage) will destroy the vampire unless the
vampire burns a blood to prevent destruction.

Any aggravated damage in excess of the first point applied to a vampire
follows the "wounded vampire" rules above, since the first point of
aggravated damage was not healed (since aggravated damage cannot be healed).

> Next: can you explain why only 1 point has to be aggravated?

Yes: see above. If you take normal damage that you cannot heal (that is,
more than you have blood with which to heal), then you have unhealed
damage. Aggravted damage done to a vampire with unhealed damage requires
the vampire to burn a blood to prevent destruction.

So, with X blood, if you take X+1 normal damage and 1 aggravated, the
normal damage will use up all of your blood and have enough left over to
wound you, and the single point of aggravated will destroy you.

> This seems
> to make no sense. Jyhad: If a vampire takes X damage, at least 2 points
> of which are aggravated, then he must burn X-1 blood or be burned.

Because, in Jyhad, the first point of agg (from each individual source)
would not destroy a vampire, wounded or not.

> So, the difference would be that now you need only one aggravated to burn.

Once you are wounded, yes.

> IMO, that's a bit tricky to explain. Especially to newbies,

Then use Gomi's ends-based explanation for newbies.

> as the first
> point of aggravated burns no blood;

unless done to a wounded vampire, in which case it "burns a blood".

> and if you have no blood to burn and
> take normal damage, you burn no additional blood and go to torpor.

The normal damage is handled first (before the agg damage).

> Please clarify these points, in *very* simple words (please).

Stop using the "first" modifier, and it can be done *very* simply.
Damage is damage. The first, last, and in-between points of damage are
all treated the same way:

A vampire with unhealed damage is said to be "wounded".
Regular damage can be healed by the vampire burning a blood to heal.
Aggravated damage cannot be healed.
Aggravated damage done to a wounded vampire will destroy the vampire
unless he burns a blood to prevent destruction.

--
L. Scott Johnson (vte...@wizards.com) VTES Net.Rep for Wizards of the Coast.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Sat, 8 Aug 1998, Doktorow/Björklund wrote:

> We (the Swedish Section) have to say that the 7/7 was great, it
> fixed many broken cards.
>

> BUT, we really don't understand the new aggr. dam. rule.
> Please describe it in another way (examples).

Well, I'm sure someone gave you the short explanation. Here's a long one.

In Jyhad, taking damage is not the same as losing blood. Rather, blood is
a resource that can be used to heal damage.

It does not take alot of damage to stop a vampire. One damage will kill
many allies and send any vampire to torpor. Two damage will kill almost
any ally. If aggravated, two damage will *destroy* any vampire.

The vampires supernatual toughness comes not from his physical
composition, but from his ability to heal the damage immediately as he
receives it, using blood as a supernatural resource. Thus, if I am a
vampire with 3 blood and someone slaps me for one damage, this would have
probably been enough to kill me had I still been mortal. However, I
instantly burn one blood and the damage is gone. I pull the dagger out of
my eyesocket and stand there just as healthy and whole as before, with no
damage, but looking perhaps a little less rosy.

Had I taken 4 damage with that slap, I would have only had enough blood to
heal 3, so I would have remained messed up. Thus I would have gone into
torpor.

Aggravated damage shocks the system so that you cannot instantly burn
blood to heal. If I have a blood supply of 10, and I take one aggravated
damage, I am then unable to burn blood to heal the damage, so I go into
torpor. Since I was not able to burn a blood to heal, I still have all
ten blood points.

Two or more points of aggravated damage, unhealed, will destroy a vampire.
The first point sends him into torpor and shuts down his system, and the
second one destroys him. However, after the first point torporized him,
he is then allowed to burn blood to heal any additional points of
aggravated damage and so prevent destruction.

Thus, if I have 10 blood and take 2 ag damage: The first point sends me
into torpor with 10 blood; the second point is healed in torpor by burning
an additional blood. Thus...I end up in torpor with 9 blood.

If a vampire is ever in a situation where he does not have sufficient
blood to heal that second point, he is burned.

Lupus Australis

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at wrote:
> vte...@wizards.com (LSJ) wrote:
> > CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at wrote:
> > > vte...@wizards.com (LSJ) wrote:
>
> > A vampire with unhealed damage is said to be "wounded".
> > Regular damage can be healed by the vampire burning a blood to heal.
> > Aggravated damage cannot be healed.
>
> Does this mean that if you take e.g. 5 aggravated damage, you burn _no_
> blood??? The last two sentences imply that.
>
> > Aggravated damage done to a wounded vampire will destroy the vampire

> > unless he burns a blood to prevent destruction.

No. You burn no blood to heal (since the aggravated damage cannot be
healed), but you burn four blood to prevent destruction.

Start:
5 aggravated damage left.
Handle one point of agg: cannot be healed, but will not destroy the vampire.
The vampire is wounded (has unhealed damage, is going to torpor).
4 aggravated damage left.
Handle one point of agg: cannot be healed, will destroy the vampire since
he is already wounded. He burns a blood to prevent destruction.
3 aggravated damage left.
Handle one point of agg: cannot be healed, will destroy the vampire since
he is already wounded. He burns a blood to prevent destruction.
2 aggravated damage left.
Handle one point of agg: cannot be healed, will destroy the vampire since
he is already wounded. He burns a blood to prevent destruction.
1 aggravated damage left.
Handle one point of agg: cannot be healed, will destroy the vampire since
he is already wounded. He burns a blood to prevent destruction.
No damage left.
The vampire, if he has not been destroyed (i.e., was able to burn a blood
to prevent destruction four times - above), then he is now placed in
torpor.

Messages.Author: Frederic Genest
Messages.Body:
In article <7xemulf...@termiitti.akumiitti.fi>,
or...@termiitti.akumiitti.fi says...


The way I understand it right now would be as follow:

A ready vampire who is dealt normal damage must burn one blood per damage
to soak it. If it cannot soak all the damage, it is sent to torpor. If
it is already going to torpor, it must still soak the damage.

A vampire without blood going to torpor ignores normal damage which is
dealt to it.

Example: A vampire with 3 blood is dealt 3 normal damage. It will burn 2
blood to soak it, and will thus be at 0 blood.

Example: A vampire with 1 blood who is dealt 3 normal damage will burn
its last blood to soak 1 damage. There will be unsoaked damage, so the
vampire is sent to torpor (at 0 blood), and the last 2 normal damage have
no other effect.

(So far, so good; typical VtES rule.)

A ready vampire who is dealt aggravated damage will soak the first point
of aggravated damage by going to torpor.

A vampire going to torpor who is dealt aggravated damage must soak the
damage by burning one blood for each aggravated damage. If it cannot
soak all the aggravated damage, it is burnt.

Example: A vampire with 3 blood is dealt 3 aggravated damage. The
vampire goes to torpor to soak the first point. There remains aggravated
damage; since the vampire is on his way to torpor, it must burn 2 blood
to soak the rest of it. Thus the vampire ends up in torpor with 1 blood.

Example: A vampire with 1 blood is dealt 3 aggravated damage. The
vampire goes to torpor to soak the first point of aggravated damage. It
then burns its last blood to soak another aggravated damage. There is
still aggravated damage to soak, so the vampire is burnt.

If a vampire is simultaneously dealt normal and aggravated damage, the

normal damage is handled first.

Example: A vampire with 1 blood is in combat against Zach North who has a
Wolf Companion. Zach uses Wolf Claws to make his hand damage aggravated.
Thus, at strike resolution, the opposing vampire is dealt 1 normal
damage, and 2 aggravated damage; normal damage is handled first. The
vampire burns his last blood to soak the normal damage. The first
aggravated damage sends the vampire in torpor, and the last one burns it.

Example: A Tremere with 1 blood is in combat against a Malkavian
Antitribu. The Tremere plays normal Weather Control and Burst of
Sunlight, while the !Malk strikes with Coma. Coma sends the Tremere in
torpor first. Then, the Tremere must soak the normal damage; thus it as
no blood remaining. It must now handle the aggravated damage; since it
is already going to torpor, and as no blood left, it is burnt.

(Well, I hope I got it right. :)

Frederic.

Messages.Author: ber...@cco.caltech.edu
Messages.Body:
> It seems we need a *simple* and *comprehensive* text about how
> aggravated damage now works. Even I'm confused by it, and I've been
> playing this game for a long time. The latest bit combining Coma and
> aggra damage shattered my illusions of understanding the new rule...
>

> We *really* need something to give to newbies (and old-timers) to
> clear this up. A major game mechanic should not be this complicated to
> understand.
>

Simple...

---Start simple agg damage rules---
All normal damage is handled before agg damage.

For a ready minion (who is not on his way to torpor): 1 point of normal
causes him to burn 1 blood. If he cannot, he goes to torpor. 1 point of agg
damage sends him to torpor.

For a minion in torpor or on his way to torpor:
1 point of normal causes him to burn 1 blood. If he cannot, no effect.
1 point of agg damage causes him to burn 1 blood. If he cannot, he burns.
---End simple agg damage rules---

I can't see it getting any simpler than that. Much easier than the old Jyhad
rules, in fact. The only caveat here is that when a ready minion takes
damage that sends him to torpor, he is considered "on his way to torpor," and
is not actually in torpor until all damage resolves. So, if a minion is
burned while on his way to torpor, he's never considered to actually be in
torpor. Note that strikes which say "Strike: the opposing minion goes to
torpor," cause the minion to be "on his way to torpor" during damage
resolution. I think that the general rule is that these types of effects are
handled before damage is dealt, so a Dawn Op/Murder of Crows will then cause
the "on his way to torpor" minion to burn a blood. (This is the only point
where I'm unsure. But seriously... how often are you going to have 1 minion
play Coma/Entombment and deal agg damage to the other minion during the same
strike resolution? Anyway, a simple ruling will clear up that timing quite
easily.)

This is the way that my playgroup has always played the game (up to the point
where V:TES rules changed agg damage). We never knew about the "packeting"
garbage that cause so much crap before. Why a vampire should care whether it
gets hit with 2 agg damage from a Walk of Flame or 2 agg damage from 2
separate Pulled Fangs is beyond me.

-Chris

> Simple...
>
> ---Start simple agg damage rules---
> All normal damage is handled before agg damage.
>
> For a ready minion (who is not on his way to torpor): 1 point of normal
> causes him to burn 1 blood. If he cannot, he goes to torpor. 1 point of agg
> damage sends him to torpor.
>
> For a minion in torpor or on his way to torpor:
> 1 point of normal causes him to burn 1 blood. If he cannot, no effect.
> 1 point of agg damage causes him to burn 1 blood. If he cannot, he burns.
> ---End simple agg damage rules---

Yes, Yes, Yes! You win the "most simple aggravated damage rules explanation"
contest! :)

in an excellent (but definitely longer) way.

> > Example: A Tremere with 1 blood is in combat against a Malkavian
> > Antitribu. The Tremere plays normal Weather Control and Burst of
> > Sunlight, while the !Malk strikes with Coma. Coma sends the Tremere in
> > torpor first. Then, the Tremere must soak the normal damage; thus it as
> > no blood remaining. It must now handle the aggravated damage; since it
> > is already going to torpor, and as no blood left, it is burnt.

> wait until I've read the others.

Thanks. :)
It is long though... I also like Gomi's and Chris'. :)

As a side note, I noticed a small mistake in my example above (though it
doesn't change the conclusion). The damage from WC is applied before
range is determined, so the order of "damage resolution" would be WC,
Coma and BoS. But the end result is the same...

Regarding why the rule may be complicated to understand. I believe it is
so for many because of the introduction of new terms such as "wounded"
and "unhealed damage"... Those terms needed to be defined/clarified
before being used in a rule, and those definitions were sorely lacking.

Gomi did that, giving us nice clarifications, which help understand his
summary afterwards. In my explanation, I didn't use those terms, and
used well known ones instead, which avoided some confusion.

Frederic.
